title: The last words
tomorrow: and if you wake at 3 a.m. anyway, what then?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my evening, closed the same way every night. That was the week of the evening: three lines, one kind word, put it down, screens off, together, my evening. One piece is left: the very last thing you say.
screen: `MY EVENING.` → `THE WEEK OF THE EVENING.` → `ONE PIECE LEFT.`

segments.voice: Fall asleep to a podcast, and the last voice of the day belongs to a stranger. A companion of the Prophet named al-Bara' was given another last voice: his own. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told him: when you go to bed, make wudu as you would for prayer, lie down on your right side, and say: O God, I hand myself over to you, I entrust my affairs to you, I lean my back on you. I believe in your Book which you sent down, and your Prophet whom you sent. Make these the last words you say. Al-Bara' repeated it back to him, and changed one word. Instead of your Prophet, he said your Messenger.
screen: `A STRANGER'S VOICE, LAST.` → `WUDU, THEN THE RIGHT SIDE.` → `I HAND MYSELF OVER TO YOU.` → `ONE WORD CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The Prophet stopped him. No, he said: your Prophet whom you sent. It's a small correction, and it says a lot. Muslim scholars have offered reasons for it; one reading is simply that words of remembrance are kept the way they were taught, not improved on the spot. This is a real Muslim practice: the supplication at bedtime, said lying on the right side, as the last words of the day. And the hadith adds something tender. If you die that night, the Prophet said, you die on the fitra, the pure, natural state a person is born with. So sleep is pictured as a small letting go, and the last words are trust: I lean my back on you. That's the shape the whole week has been building. Read a little, mend what needs mending, set the worry down, put the light out, eat together, close the evening. Then one line, the same one every night, kept word for word. Not something new to think about. Something to rest on.
screen: `NO: YOUR PROPHET WHOM YOU SENT.` · `KEPT THE WAY IT WAS TAUGHT.` · `SAID LYING ON THE RIGHT SIDE.` · `I LEAN MY BACK ON YOU.` · then, large: `THE LAST WORDS.`

segments.voice: Choose your last words: the Prophet's, if you're Muslim, a line from your own tradition, or one plain sentence of trust you could say every night. Say it out loud once, slowly, exactly the way you mean to keep it. Then let nothing come after it but your breathing.
The last words: one fixed line said as the very last thing before sleep, kept word for word, the way al-Bara' was taught.
Your line: the last words, the same ones, every night, word for word. Seven evenings, one week, done.

screen: `DAY 1617 COUNTS.` → `THE WEEK OF THE EVENING · 7 CARDS · THE DAILY PRACTICE 21 OF 23.` → `TOMORROW: AND IF YOU WAKE AT 3 A.M. ANYWAY, WHAT THEN?`

howItsDone: Muslims learn the Prophet's bedtime practice from this hadith: wudu, lying on the right side, and this supplication as the last words before sleep.

al-Bara'.meaning: al-Bara' ibn Azib, a companion of the Prophet

wudu.meaning: the washing Muslims do before prayer

fitra.meaning: Arabic: the pure, natural state a person is born with

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 247 (al-Bara' ibn Azib: wudu before bed, lying on the right side, the supplication; 'make them the last words you say'; dying that night on the fitra; 'your Prophet whom you sent', not 'your Messenger')
